entry.title: Singapore's FirstDate Pilot Uses Gale-Shapley Algorithm to Match Public Officers
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | singapore-samizdat.com | source | hacker news

GovTech has launched a pilot dating service for Singaporean public officers aged 21 to 35. The platform uses Singpass for identity verification and employs the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage Algorithm to facilitate matchmaking in programmatic cycles. Users are required to complete an extensive questionnaire covering lifestyle, values, and communication styles to determine their ranked preferences.

Critics argue that applying the Gale-Shapley algorithm to romance may fail to address the core complexities of modern dating. The model prioritizes mathematical stability—ensuring participants do not prefer other assigned partners—over emotional or holistic compatibility. Furthermore, the reliance on self-reported data and the existence of non-participating "outside options" may undermine the algorithm's effectiveness in a real-world social context.

entry.title: Pew Research Center Survey Finds Growing Global Concern That Social Media Harms Democracy
entry.content:
Techmeme | pewresearch.org | hacker news

A Pew Research Center survey across 37 countries reveals that more people globally believe social media is harming democracy. In most nations with trend data, the share of citizens who view social media as a "bad thing" for democracy has increased since 2022 or 2023. In the United States, 64% of adults view social media as bad for democracy, a sentiment that has remained unchanged since 2022.

Negative perceptions are more prevalent in wealthier nations, such as Canada, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States. In contrast, residents in lower GDP per capita countries, such as Ghana, Kenya, and Nigeria, are more likely to view social media as a positive force for democracy. Findings also show that younger adults in most nations tend to be more optimistic about social media's impact than older generations.

entry.title: Complex Traveling Waves in the Brain Support Cognitive Tasks
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | quantamagazine.org | hacker news

Electrical waves traveling through the brain exhibit complex patterns, including source, sink, and rotating spiral waves, rather than simple planar oscillations. Research in humans and mice shows that these diverse wave structures correlate with specific cognitive activities, such as verbal and spatial memory.

These dynamic patterns may enable the brain to reorganize neural activity in real time to meet behavioral demands, acting as a functional layer of organization distinct from stable anatomical connections. While some scientists argue these waves are reflections of underlying synaptic activity, others suggest they play crucial roles in sensory prediction and inter-regional communication.

entry.title: Iron Technology and the Bronze Age Collapse
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | worksinprogress.news | hacker news

The transition from bronze to iron technology was a primary driver of the Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BC. While centralized empires maintained dominance by controlling long-distance tin trade routes, the ability to produce iron locally using bloomery furnaces decentralized access to military tools. This shift fundamentally undermined the political and military monopolies previously held by large, bureaucratically complex states.

Traditional explanations for the collapse often cite droughts, famines, or invasions, but the shift to iron explains why large empires failed to re-emerge for centuries. The widespread availability of iron allowed even peripheral communities to equip effective fighting forces, preventing the re-consolidation of political power into massive imperial structures.

Adopting a collegial tone serves as an operational method to steer models into the high-quality, academic, or technical domains of their training data.

entry.content:

entry.title: Limits of AI Expertise in Assessing Existential Risks
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | bcantrill.dtrace.org | discussion | hacker news

The article argues that "AI doomerism" is often fueled by "fool's expertise," a phenomenon where AI researchers make unsubstantiated claims about catastrophic risks in domains outside their specialized knowledge. Using Geoffrey Hinton's inaccurate prediction about the obsolescence of radiologists as a primary example, the author contends that proficiency in artificial intelligence does not confer authority to predict failures in complex, real-world systems like biology, cybersecurity, or nuclear safety.

The author advocates for a domain-specific approach to assessing AI-related extinction risks, citing a RAND Corporation study that prioritized experts in nuclear weapons, biotechnology, and climate change over AI specialists. By focusing on the specific physical mechanisms and established safeguards of various sectors, the author suggests that the discourse on catastrophic risk becomes more grounded and less speculative.
